# Multivariable Models {#sec-multivariable}

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("_common.R")
brfss_clean <- readRDS(file.path(processed_dir, "02-brfss-clean.rds"))
imputed <- readRDS(file.path(processed_dir, "04-imputed.rds"))
crude <- readRDS(file.path(processed_dir, "05-crude.rds"))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  cache.extra = c(
    cache_context,
    list(
      data = tools::md5sum(file.path(
        processed_dir,
        c("02-brfss-clean.rds", "04-imputed.rds", "05-crude.rds")
      ))
    )
  )
)
```

The crude prevalence ratios in @sec-bivariate mix the association of income with the
associations of everything that travels with income. Age is the clearest example: adults 65
and older are less likely than middle-aged adults to have a high household income (many are
retired) and far more likely to have diabetes. A multivariable model estimates the association of income with
diabetes **among adults of the same age group, sex, and race and ethnicity**.

## Helpers

The three helper functions are the same as in @sec-bivariate.

```{r}
#| label: helpers
# Fit one model per completed dataset; keep the estimates, their covariance matrix, and the
# residual degrees of freedom. Each design is built, used, and discarded in turn.
fit_each <- function(imputed, formula) {
  purrr::map(seq_len(imputed$m), \(i) {
    design <- mice::complete(imputed, i) |>
      dplyr::mutate(diabetes_yes = as.integer(diabetes == "Yes")) |>
      srvyr::as_survey_design(
        ids = psu_id,
        strata = strata,
        weights = weight,
        check_strata = FALSE
      )
    fit <- survey::svyglm(
      formula,
      design = design,
      family = stats::quasipoisson()
    )
    list(
      coef = stats::coef(fit),
      vcov = stats::vcov(fit),
      df = stats::df.residual(fit)
    )
  })
}

pool_fits <- function(fits) {
  estimates <- purrr::map(fits, \(fit) {
    tibble::tibble(
      term = names(fit$coef),
      estimate = fit$coef,
      std.error = sqrt(diag(fit$vcov)),
      df.residual = fit$df
    )
  })
  mice::pool.table(purrr::list_rbind(estimates), exponentiate = TRUE)
}

format_pr <- function(pooled) {
  pooled |>
    tibble::as_tibble() |>
    dplyr::filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      term,
      `PR (95% CI)` = sprintf(
        "%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)",
        estimate,
        conf.low,
        conf.high
      ),
      p = format.pval(p.value, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)
    )
}
```

## The adjusted model

The model has all four predictors at once.

```{r}
#| label: adjusted
#| cache: true
adjusted_fits <- fit_each(
  imputed,
  diabetes_yes ~ income + age_group + sex + race_eth
)
adjusted <- pool_fits(adjusted_fits)

dplyr::left_join(
  format_pr(crude),
  format_pr(adjusted),
  by = dplyr::join_by(term),
  suffix = c(", crude", ", adjusted")
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = paste0(
      "Table 4. Crude and adjusted prevalence ratios for diabetes (",
      n_imputations,
      " imputations)"
    )
  )
```

Each adjusted PR compares two groups that are alike on the other variables in the model. For
example, the PR for `income$100,000 or more` compares adults in the highest income group
with adults earning less than $25,000 *of the same age group, sex, and race and ethnicity*.

## Does income matter overall?

Income has four groups, so it has three PRs, each with its own p-value. To ask whether income
is associated with diabetes at all, we test the three coefficients together (null
hypothesis: all three are zero on the log scale). `mitml::testConstraints()` runs this
multivariate Wald test across imputations (the "D1" statistic, pooled with Rubin's rules)
from each dataset's estimates and covariance matrix.

```{r}
#| label: joint-test
income_terms <- grep("^income", names(adjusted_fits[[1]]$coef), value = TRUE)
income_test <- mitml::testConstraints(
  qhat = do.call(cbind, purrr::map(adjusted_fits, "coef")),
  uhat = simplify2array(purrr::map(adjusted_fits, \(fit) fit$vcov)),
  constraints = paste0("`", income_terms, "`"), # backticks: the names contain spaces
  method = "D1"
)
income_test
```

`df1` is the number of coefficients tested and `P(>F)` the p-value.

## Sensitivity analysis: complete cases

How much did imputation change the results? The same model fit to complete cases drops
everyone with a missing value. `survey::svyglm()` keeps the full design for the variance and
gives the dropped respondents no weight in the estimates.

```{r}
#| label: complete-case
#| cache: true
complete_case <- survey::svyglm(
  diabetes_yes ~ income + age_group + sex + race_eth,
  design = srvyr::as_survey_design(
    brfss_clean,
    ids = psu_id,
    strata = strata,
    weights = weight,
    check_strata = FALSE
  ),
  family = stats::quasipoisson()
)
complete_case_pr <- broom::tidy(
  complete_case,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  exponentiate = TRUE
)
complete_case_n <- stats::nobs(complete_case)
rm(complete_case) # Cache the small results, not the full model object.

dplyr::left_join(
  format_pr(complete_case_pr),
  format_pr(adjusted),
  by = dplyr::join_by(term),
  suffix = c(", complete case", ", imputed")
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = paste(
      "Table 5. Adjusted prevalence ratios:",
      "complete case and multiple imputation"
    )
  )
```

The complete-case model uses `r format(complete_case_n, big.mark = ",")`
respondents; the imputed models use all `r format(nrow(brfss_clean), big.mark = ",")`.

**Where do the missing data matter?** The fraction of missing information (`fmi`) is the share
of each estimate's variance that comes from the missing data. It is highest for the income
terms, where most values were imputed, and close to zero for variables with nothing missing.

```{r}
#| label: fmi
adjusted |> dplyr::transmute(term, pr = round(estimate, 2), fmi = round(fmi, 3))
```

::: callout-important
## When the two analyses disagree

If complete-case and imputed results differ substantially, report both and explain why,
rather than choosing the one you like better. Under MAR the imputed results are the less
biased ones; if missingness might depend on income itself (MNAR), neither is guaranteed to be
right, and a sensitivity analysis for MNAR is the next step.
:::

## Reporting the results

```{r}
#| label: report-values
top_income <- dplyr::filter(adjusted, term == "income$100,000 or more")
top_income_cc <- dplyr::filter(
  complete_case_pr,
  term == "income$100,000 or more"
)
```

A results paragraph might read:

> We analyzed `r format(nrow(brfss_clean), big.mark = ",")` adults in the 2024 Behavioral Risk
> Factor Surveillance System, representing `r format(round(sum(brfss_clean$weight) / 1e6, 1))`
> million US adults. All estimates accounted for the survey weights, strata, and primary
> sampling units. Household income was missing for
> `r round(100 * mean(is.na(brfss_clean$income)), 1)`% of respondents, and missingness varied
> with age and general health. We multiply imputed missing values (`r n_imputations`
> imputations by chained equations with the `mice` package, version
> `r utils::packageVersion("mice")`, predictive mean matching, with the survey weight as a
> predictor) and pooled estimates with Rubin's rules. In a survey-weighted modified Poisson
> model adjusted for age group, sex, and race and ethnicity, adults with a household income of
> $100,000 or more had a prevalence of diabetes `r sprintf("%.2f", top_income$estimate)` times
> that of adults earning less than $25,000 (95% CI `r sprintf("%.2f", top_income$conf.low)` to
> `r sprintf("%.2f", top_income$conf.high)`; joint test of income
> p `r format.pval(income_test$test[, "P(>F)"], digits = 2, eps = 0.001)`). In a complete-case
> analysis the prevalence ratio was `r sprintf("%.2f", top_income_cc$estimate)` (95% CI
> `r sprintf("%.2f", top_income_cc$conf.low)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", top_income_cc$conf.high)`).

### Reporting checklist

For any analysis of complex survey data, report:

- [ ] the survey design (weights, strata, clusters) and that every estimate used it;
- [ ] the unweighted sample size and the weighted population;
- [ ] design-based tests (for example, Rao-Scott chi-square) and confidence intervals;
- [ ] design effects for key estimates.

When the analysis uses multiple imputation, also report:

- [ ] the amount of missing data for each variable and evidence about why it is missing;
- [ ] the imputation method for each variable, the number of imputations, and the software
  and version;
- [ ] the variables in the imputation model, including how the survey design entered it;
- [ ] that estimates were pooled with Rubin's rules;
- [ ] complete-case results next to the imputed results.

## Exercise

Repeat @sec-bivariate and this chapter for **fair or poor general health**: in `fit_each()`,
add `fair_poor = as.integer(genhlth == "Fair" | genhlth == "Poor")` next to `diabetes_yes`,
then replace `diabetes_yes` with `fair_poor` in every model formula. Everything else, including the imputed data,
can be reused. Is the income gradient steeper or flatter than for diabetes? How much does
adjustment for age change it, and why might that differ from diabetes?
